name: The Mallrat Mothman
epithet: The Thing in the Dead Wing

inspiration.oldScript: The creature in the dark that snatches children.
inspiration.newLens: The kids nobody was watching. The Mothman takes the ones the mall swallowed, and the Best ending is a town that notices.

logline: Something seven feet tall lives in the dead neon of Starlight Mall. It only takes the kids nobody is watching, and the worst part is how long it takes anyone to notice they are gone.
backstory: When Starlight Mall opened in 1974, its pride was Moonbeam Court: a skylit wing with a wishing fountain under a giant fiberglass luna moth named Mona, the mall mascot. For nine years the court was where Glimmer Falls parked its kids. Parents working double shifts, parents at the bar, parents who just forgot dropped them off at ten and came back at closing, or later, or not at all. Kids threw their last quarters in Mona's fountain and wished, over and over, for somebody to come. A gentle security guard named Earl Lusk ran the Lost Kids desk and wrote every one of them down. In 1983 the anchor store went bankrupt, the wing was boarded up with plywood, the fountain was drained and Mona was hauled to the junkyard. The wishes stayed. This Halloween week the Heartstone has woken them into a body: a moth as tall as a door, wings of dust and dead neon, eyespots like clocks stuck at closing time. It drifts through the mall and the cul-de-sacs after dark, drawn to porch lights and arcade screens, and it carries the unwatched kids back to the dead wing and wraps them in soft gray cocoons, where they sleep peacefully and wait for a grown-up who never comes.

centralIssue.title: Kids neglected and parked at the mall
centralIssue.summary: The Mothman is not a predator. It is every lonely hour Glimmer Falls kids spent waiting under the neon, given wings, and it keeps the children nobody else is keeping. Defeating it will not fix the reason those kids were alone. Find Earl's logbook, read the wishes in Mona's belly and learn which kids vanished without anyone reporting it, then make the whole town finally show up.

poster: A seven-foot moth creature with dusty pale-green wings and glowing red eyes perched on a dead neon sign in a boarded-up 1970s shopping mall wing, gray silk cocoons hanging from the skylights like lanterns, a drained wishing fountain full of quarters below, teens with flashlights creeping in through a gap in the plywood
portrait: Close portrait of a giant moth creature's face, furry gray-green mane, two huge glowing red eyes like exit signs, feathery antennae, dust drifting off its wings in a beam of neon pink light, strangely gentle and very sad
endingPhoto: A seven-foot moth creature with dusty pale-green wings and glowing red eyes crouched on the rim of a drained mall fountain, wings spread wide under a cracked skylight and a full moon, silk cocoons hanging from a dead neon sign, teens pressed against a boarded-up arcade doorway holding a flickering lantern
taunts: Attention shoppers. Will anyone please come for this child?
Nobody's coming. They never come. Stay with me.
Closing time. Lights out. Sleep, little one. Sleep.

clues.title: Earl's logbook
clues.hint: An old security guard drinks coffee in the Starlight Mall food court every single day. He used to run the Lost Kids desk in the dead wing.

encounter.title: The Lost Kids Desk
encounter.text: Earl Lusk is seventy, wears his old security blazer with the patch picked off, and sits at the same food court table every day with a coffee and a view of the plywood wall that seals off Moonbeam Court. When a kid wanders past alone, his eyes follow them all the way to the exit. A brass key hangs on a shoelace around his neck. On the plywood behind him, someone has spray-painted a moth, and its wings are dusty, and real.
encounter.art: A 70-year-old Black man in a faded navy security blazer with a pale square where a patch was picked off, a brass key on a shoelace around his neck, sitting at a mall food court table with a paper cup of coffee, behind him a tall plywood wall with a big spray-painted moth whose wings shed real gray dust onto the floor, a teenager sitting down across from him, pink and gold neon from the food stands, medium shot

choices.label: Buy him a fresh coffee and ask about the Lost Kids desk

success.text: Earl talks for an hour. Nine years, eleven hundred kids found alone at closing, and the same names, week after week. "Paged their folks three times. No answer. Walked them home myself." He slides the key off his neck. "Logbook's still in the desk. When they boarded it up, nobody asked me for it." The last page, you find later, is in his handwriting. The new pages after it are written in dust.
success.art: An elderly security guard handing a brass key across a food court table to a teenager, two coffees between them, a thick old logbook glowing faintly in the air above them like a memory

failure.text: Earl just shakes his head. "Kids don't listen. Folks don't listen. Nobody listens to Earl." He goes back to watching the exit. When you turn around, the painted moth on the plywood has moved its wings a quarter inch. You are almost sure.
failure.art: An elderly guard turning away at a food court table, a painted moth on a plywood wall with its wings shifted slightly, dust floating in the neon light

choices.label: Squeeze through the gap in the plywood and find the desk yourself

success.text: The dead wing smells like chlorine and old pretzels. The Lost Kids desk is still there, a sign above it reading WAIT HERE, SOMEONE IS COMING. In the drawer is the logbook: Rhonda, age 7, parents paged 3x, walked home. Rhonda, age 7, again. Rhonda, age 8. And this week's pages, in gray powder that smears when you touch it: Marcy H. Benji F. Tyler G. No one paged.
success.art: A teenager with a flashlight reading a thick logbook at a dusty security desk in a dark abandoned mall wing, a sign above reading wait here someone is coming, gray powdery handwriting on the newest page

failure.text: Your jacket snags on the plywood and you hang there, half in, half out, while a mall cop writes you a ticket for trespassing. From the dark side of the wall, something enormous and soft brushes past your dangling sneakers. It hums like a fluorescent light.
failure.art: A teenager stuck halfway through a gap in a plywood wall, a mall cop writing a ticket on the bright side, on the dark side a huge soft wing brushing past their sneakers

clues.title: Mona's wishes
clues.hint: When Moonbeam Court closed, the giant fiberglass moth from the fountain was hauled to Rusty's Junkyard. Kids used to post wishes in a slot in her base.

encounter.title: Mona in the Weeds
encounter.text: Mona the Moonbeam Moth lies on her side in the weeds behind the car crusher, twenty feet of cracked fiberglass with pale green wings and a smile painted for a 1974 mall opening. Under her belly is a brass slot with a sign: MAKE A MOONBEAM WISH! Somebody forgot to ever empty it. Her painted eyes are dull. Then, as a cloud crosses the sun, they very faintly glow.
encounter.art: A twenty-foot fiberglass luna moth mascot lying on its side in tall junkyard weeds behind a rusty car crusher, pale green wings cracked and peeling, a big painted 1970s smile, a brass coin slot in its belly, a teenager kneeling beside the slot with a tire iron, its painted eyes glowing faint red as a cloud shadow crosses the yard, afternoon sun and cloud shadow, wide shot

choices.label: Pry open the wish box with a tire iron

success.text: The panel pops and an avalanche of folded paper pours out, thousands of wishes in crayon and pencil. I wish my mom would come on time. I wish someone would notice I'm here. I wish I could stay at the fountain forever because at least Mona sees me. You read until the sun goes down, and you understand exactly what has been granting them.
success.art: An avalanche of folded paper wishes and quarters pouring from a cracked fiberglass moth's belly in a junkyard, a teenager kneeling to read crayon handwriting at sunset

failure.text: The tire iron slips and gashes Mona's painted wing. A sound comes out of her, low and hurt, like a mall PA system in pain. Every junked car in the maze honks at once, and you spend the next ten minutes lost in the rows.
failure.art: A tire iron sticking out of a fiberglass moth's wing, a teenager covering their ears as headlights blink on across a maze of junked cars

choices.label: Fish wishes out of the slot one at a time with a coat hanger

success.text: It takes all afternoon, but the coat hanger hooks out a fistful of notes and a few quarters. The first one says: I'm at Moonbeam Court again. It's 9:15. The gate is down. Please, somebody. It is signed by a kid you know, who is sixteen now and laughs a little too loud at the arcade. You keep that one in your pocket.
success.art: A teenager hooking folded paper notes out of a brass slot with a bent coat hanger, a small pile of wishes and quarters on the dirt, a giant moth sculpture looming over them

failure.text: Every note you fish out is blank, except the last one, which is wet and new. It reads: you're not watching either. When you look up, Rusty's guard dog is staring at the moth's head, whimpering, backing away on its belly.
failure.art: A teenager holding a fresh damp note in a junkyard, a guard dog whimpering and backing away from a giant moth sculpture's head

clues.title: The kids nobody reported
clues.hint: The paperboy on Crystal Street knows every house on his route, and which ones nobody has been home to all week.

encounter.title: Collection Day
encounter.place: Kev Park's paper route, Crystal Street
encounter.text: It is collection day on the paper route, and Kev Park is doing math on his fingers on his bike. "The Ferreiras haven't picked up a paper since Saturday. The Holcombs' porch has six. And there's a kid's bike in the Gaskins yard that hasn't moved in four days." He frowns at his notebook. "Nobody called the cops. Nobody even called me to stop delivery."
encounter.art: A skinny 12-year-old Korean American paperboy in a backwards red cap and a blue hooded sweatshirt straddling a red bicycle with a canvas sack of newspapers on a suburban cul-de-sac, counting on his fingers and pointing at a porch piled with six rolled newspapers, a child's small bike lying on an overgrown lawn, a teenager on a bike beside him, late afternoon sun, wide shot

choices.label: Ride the route with Kev and check every house

success.text: Three houses. Three kids missing since the weekend. At the Holcombs', Marcy's mother opens the door in her waitress uniform, exhausted. "She's at the mall. She's always at the mall." Then she counts the days on her fingers and her face slowly falls apart. Kev writes all three names on the back of a collection envelope and hands it to you.
success.art: A tired mother in a waitress uniform at a front door counting on her fingers with dawning horror, a teenager and a paperboy on the step holding a collection envelope with names written on it

failure.text: You pedal hard and still miss the end of the route by dark. The porch lights come on one by one, and above the Gaskins house, something huge blocks out the stars for a moment and is gone. Kev pedals home so fast he leaves his bag behind.
failure.art: Two kids on bikes on a dusky suburban street, porch lights blinking on, a vast winged shape crossing in front of the stars above a rooftop, a dropped newspaper bag on the curb

choices.label: Read what's piled up on the Gaskins porch

success.text: Newspapers. A note taped to the door: TYLER, MOM ON DOUBLES TILL SUNDAY, MONEY FOR MALL IN JAR. A jar with three dollars in it. And on the welcome mat, a trail of gray-green dust leading from the door to the street, as if someone very large and very soft walked a small child away by the hand.
success.art: A suburban porch with a stack of unread newspapers, a taped note on the door, a jar with a few dollar bills, and a trail of glittering gray-green dust leading from the welcome mat to the street

failure.text: A neighbor sees you on the porch and assumes the worst, of you. By the time you have explained yourself, it is getting dark, and the porch light above you clicks on by itself. Something big taps against it, once, softly, like a moth.
failure.art: A suspicious neighbor in curlers pointing at a teenager on a stranger's porch at dusk, the porch light above them clicking on with a huge soft shadow bumping against it

signature.title: Closing Time
signature.text: The security gates rattle down storefront by storefront. The PA chimes: "Will the parent of Tyler, age eight, please come to the arcade." Nobody comes. In the arcade a small boy is playing the attract screen of a machine with no quarters, pretending. The lights go out one wing at a time. Above the skylight, something as big as a car settles onto the glass, and dust drifts down through the cracks like snow.
signature.art: A shopping mall at nine at night, metal security gates rattling down over storefronts and one wing going dark, a small eight-year-old boy alone at an arcade cabinet pretending to play its glowing demo screen with empty pockets turned out, a teenager walking toward him, above them on the glass skylight the dark shape of a moth as big as a car settling down, gray dust falling through the cracks in the skylight, blue arcade glow, wide shot

choices.label: Take Tyler's hand and get him out before the lights go

success.text: You give Tyler a quarter for later and walk him out the employee exit, talking the whole time about anything: monster trucks, cereal, whether moths can see colors. In the parking lot he squeezes your hand. "Nobody walks with me usually." Behind you, the shape on the skylight shifts and does not follow.
success.art: A teenager walking a small boy across a mall parking lot at night holding his hand, the boy clutching a quarter, a giant moth on the skylight behind them watching and keeping their distance

failure.text: The lights cut out and Tyler's hand slips out of yours. For three terrible minutes you shout his name in the dark. You find him asleep on a bench by the drained fountain, tucked under a blanket of soft gray dust, unharmed. He opens one eye. "The big moth said you'd forget me too."
failure.art: A small boy asleep on a mall bench beside a drained fountain under a blanket of soft gray dust, a frantic teen with a dying flashlight finding him in the dark

choices.label: Hide in the photo booth and get a picture of the thing

success.text: You yank the curtain shut and feed in your last quarter. Flash, flash, flash, flash. The strip that drops out shows four frames of the mall behind you, and in the last one, a furry gray face with two red exit-sign eyes, looking right into the lens, curious. You have proof. You also have chills that will not stop.
success.art: A strip of four photo booth pictures, the last frame showing a furry moth creature with glowing red eyes peering curiously into the camera behind a startled teen

failure.text: The flash goes off, and a moth cannot resist a light. The whole booth rocks as something lands on its roof. A long feathery antenna slides in under the curtain and touches your cheek, gently, the way you would check if a sleeping kid is breathing. Then it is gone.
failure.art: A photo booth rocking in a dark mall corridor with a giant moth perched on its roof, a feathery antenna slipping under the curtain toward a frozen teen

signature.title: Porch Lights
signature.place: The Alvarado house, Crystal Street, eleven p.m.
signature.text: It comes to Crystal Street. Every porch light on the cul-de-sac flickers as the Mothman glides overhead, slow and huge, wings whispering. It lands on the Alvarados' roof. On the front steps below sits ten-year-old Ricky Alvarad in his pajamas, waiting for his parents to get home from the cannery's late shift, the way he does every night. He is looking up at it. He is not scared. That is the scary part.
signature.art: A huge moth creature with dusty gray-green wings and two glowing red eyes perched on the roof of a split-level house at eleven at night, wings spread over a suburban street where every porch light flickers, a ten-year-old boy in pajamas sitting alone on the front steps below, chin in his hands, looking up at it calmly, a teenager coming up the sidewalk, flickering yellow porch light and blue moonlight, wide shot from the street

choices.label: Sit down on the steps next to Ricky and wait with him

success.text: You sit. You trade a stick of gum for the story of every car that is not his parents'. Up on the roof the Mothman watches the two of you for a long time, then lifts off and drifts away. It only takes the kids who are alone. Ricky's mom pulls in at 1 a.m. and hugs him so hard his feet leave the ground.
success.art: A teenager and a small boy sitting together on front steps at night sharing gum, a giant moth lifting off a roof and drifting away, headlights pulling into the driveway

failure.text: Ricky does not want company. "Mom says don't talk to strangers." He goes inside and locks the door, and you stand on the lawn while the Mothman crawls down the side of the house to his bedroom window and taps on the glass, softly, again and again.
failure.art: A giant moth creature clinging to the side of a house tapping on a lit bedroom window, a teen helpless on the lawn below

choices.label: Run the cul-de-sac turning off every porch light

success.text: Your crew splits up and unscrews bulbs house by house. Crystal Street goes dark, porch by porch, until only the Heartstone glows purple in the roundabout. The Mothman lifts off, confused, and drifts toward it, circling the geode like a lamp until dawn, harmless and mesmerized.
success.art: Teens unscrewing porch light bulbs on a darkening cul-de-sac, a giant moth circling a glowing purple geode in the roundabout like a lamp

failure.text: Mr. Dombrowski catches you unscrewing his porch bulb and turns on every light in his house in protest. The Mothman pivots toward the blaze, and its wing brushes you as it passes. For an hour afterward, you feel completely, perfectly invisible.
failure.art: An angry neighbor in a bathrobe in a fully lit doorway, a giant moth swooping toward the light, its dusty wing brushing a teenager on the lawn

choices.label: Flash a light and run, so it follows you instead

success.text: You click the beam on and off and sprint down the street. The Mothman follows, enchanted, gliding over your head, past the last house, out over the dark foothills. When you finally switch off your light at the edge of town, it circles once, gently, and flies away toward the mall.
success.art: A teenager sprinting down a dark suburban road waving a flashlight beam, a giant moth gliding overhead following the light out toward the dark foothills

failure.text: It follows you, all right. It follows you all the way home and settles on your roof. You lie awake until dawn listening to its wings breathe against the shingles, and in the morning there is a perfect dusty outline of a moth on your bedroom window.
failure.art: A dusty outline of a giant moth on the outside of a bedroom window at sunrise, a sleepless teen staring at it from bed

signature.title: Have You Seen Me?
signature.place: The all-night Quik-Stop on Quarry Road, 1 a.m.
signature.text: You stop at the all-night Quik-Stop for a Bolt Cola, and the dairy case is wrong. Every milk carton has a kid's face printed on the side under HAVE YOU SEEN ME?, and they are faces you know from the arcade, the food court, the bus stop. Their mouths move. They are whispering their own names, so softly you can barely hear. The clerk has his headphones on and has not looked up once. On the roof, something heavy shifts, and gray dust sifts past the front window like snow.
signature.art: A fluorescent-lit all-night convenience store at one in the morning, a teenager standing at an open glass dairy case full of milk cartons printed with small children's faces with their small mouths open, a young clerk in big headphones flipping through a magazine at the counter, gray dust drifting down past the front window from the roof, white fluorescent light and dark parking lot outside, medium wide shot

choices.label: Slide off the clerk's headphones and make him look

success.text: You set a carton on the counter and ease his headphones off. "Look. Do you know her?" The clerk, Rudy, squints, and then his face falls. "That's Marcy. She bought gum here every Saturday, until she didn't." He picks up the phone to call it in. On the roof, the heavy thing shifts once more and goes still, as if it is listening.
success.art: A teenager holding up a milk carton to a startled convenience-store clerk with headphones around his neck at 1 a.m., fluorescent lights, a glowing dairy case behind, gray dust drifting past the front window

failure.text: Rudy glances at the carton and shrugs. "Kids run off. Their folks'll call." He puts his headphones back on. On every carton in the case, the faces turn away from you, and the whispering stops, which is worse than the whispering.
failure.art: A bored convenience-store clerk in headphones ignoring a teenager at 1 a.m., a dairy case behind them full of milk cartons with tiny printed faces turned away, gray dust sifting past the window

choices.label: Follow the trail of dust around back

success.text: The dust leads past the dumpsters to the loading dock, where a boy in a too-big jacket is curled up asleep on a pile of flattened boxes. Crouched over him, wings folded like a tent, is the Mothman. It looks at you with eyes like exit signs. Then, slowly, it steps back and lets you wake him and walk him inside to the warm.
success.art: A towering moth creature with folded dusty wings and glowing red eyes crouched protectively over a boy asleep on flattened boxes at a store loading dock at night, a teenager approaching with a flashlight

failure.text: Your flashlight lands on two red eyes the size of hubcaps, and the light is exactly what it wanted. It lifts off with a sound like a hundred pages turning, and dust pours over you in a cloud. When you can see again, the loading dock is empty and your flashlight is coated gray.
failure.art: A teenager coughing in a cloud of gray dust on a store loading dock at night, a flashlight beam caught on two huge glowing red eyes above, enormous dusty wings beating overhead

choices.label: Buy every carton and take them to the police station

success.text: You empty your pockets on the counter and wheel forty cartons of milk out in a shopping cart. At the station you line them up along the front desk, faces out, and the night officer starts counting the kids nobody ever filed a report on. By dawn there is a list. It is a long list.
success.art: A teenager pushing a shopping cart heaped with milk cartons into a small-town police station at dawn, an officer at the front desk staring at a long row of cartons lined up face out

failure.text: You get the cartons as far as the door, and every one of them is suddenly ordinary: a cartoon cow, a sale price, and that is all. Rudy makes you pay anyway. You drink milk for a week, and every glass tastes faintly of dust.
failure.art: A glum teenager at a kitchen table surrounded by a towering stack of ordinary milk cartons with cartoon cows, a glass of milk in hand, morning light through the window

signature.title: Ready or Not
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls Elementary playground, 1 a.m.
signature.text: The swings at Glimmer Falls Elementary are moving on a windless night. All across the playground, little kids in pajamas are hiding: behind the tube slide, under the merry-go-round, curled in the tire tunnel, giggling. A voice is counting through the dark, slow and buzzing, like a voice played through a box fan: "Ninety-seven. Ninety-eight." On top of the jungle gym, the Mothman has its huge wings folded over its eyes. It is It. It is the only one who ever comes looking for them.
signature.art: A moonlit elementary school playground at one in the morning, empty swings swaying on a still night, small children in pajamas hiding behind a tube slide, under a merry-go-round and inside a tire tunnel with grinning faces, on top of the jungle gym a giant moth creature with dusty gray-green wings folded over its face, feathery antennae up, a teenager standing at the edge of the playground, blue moonlight, wide shot

choices.label: Play to win: find every kid before it opens its eyes

success.text: You know every hiding spot on this playground; you were a kid here. Tube slide, tire tunnel, behind the dumpster, inside the rocket. You round up seven sleepy kids before the voice reaches a hundred, and when the Mothman lowers its wings, the only one left to find is you. It looks at you a long time, then tags your shoulder, gently, and flies away.
success.art: A teenager leading a line of sleepy small kids in pajamas across a moonlit school playground, a giant moth creature atop a jungle gym lowering its dusty wings to look, swings swaying gently

failure.text: "One hundred. Ready or not." The wings open, and every hidden kid squeals with delight and runs to it, not away. By the time you reach the jungle gym they are all fast asleep under its wings in a soft gray heap, and it hisses at you like a goose guarding goslings.
failure.art: A heap of small kids in pajamas asleep under the spread dusty wings of a giant moth creature on a playground at night, the creature hissing at a teenager like a guarding goose

choices.label: Crawl into the tire tunnel and keep the littlest kid company

success.text: Inside the tunnel is a girl named Rosie, maybe six, hugging a stuffed rabbit. "I'm winning," she whispers, "because nobody ever finds me." You tell her you found her, and that being found is how you win hide-and-seek. She thinks about it and takes your hand. When the wings open, the Mothman finds the two of you together and leaves you be.
success.art: A teenager and a little girl with a stuffed rabbit crouched inside a playground tire tunnel at night, holding hands and smiling, the dusty wingtip and glowing red eye of a huge moth creature peering in

failure.text: Rosie shoves you. "You'll give us away!" She scrambles out the far end toward the jungle gym, and you crawl after her too slowly. When you come out, gray dust is drifting down the slide, and every kid on the playground is gone, along with the thing that was counting.
failure.art: A teenager crawling out of a playground tire tunnel at night onto bare wood chips, gray dust drifting down a metal slide, swings creaking, a stuffed rabbit lying alone in the sand

choices.label: Stand in the open and shout "Olly olly oxen free!"

success.text: You climb onto the merry-go-round and bellow the magic words loud enough to wake the block. Game over, everybody home. The kids pop out of their hiding places, yawning, and porch lights snap on across the street as parents come out in bathrobes, calling names. On the jungle gym, the Mothman unfolds its wings and drifts away, as if relieved its shift is over.
success.art: A teenager standing on a playground merry-go-round shouting with cupped hands at night, small kids in pajamas popping out of hiding, porch lights glowing across the street, a giant moth flying away

failure.text: Your voice cracks halfway through and comes out a squeak. The kids laugh at you from every hiding place. The Mothman laughs too, a dry, papery rattle, and the game goes on, and on, until dawn sends everyone home.
failure.art: A red-faced teenager on a playground merry-go-round at night, giggling kids peeking from behind a slide and a tire tunnel, a giant moth creature atop the jungle gym shaking with papery laughter

signature.title: Something in the Mirror
signature.place: Your bathroom mirror, 1 a.m., home alone
signature.text: Everyone at your house is working late tonight. The note on the fridge says pizza money is on the counter, and the house is so quiet you can hear the refrigerator think. Brushing your teeth, you notice fine gray fuzz on your shoulders and two feathery antennae curling out of your bangs. In the mirror your pupils catch the light and glow red. Downstairs, the porch light keeps clicking on by itself, and you want, very badly, to go and stand under it.
signature.art: A teenager brushing their teeth at a small bathroom mirror at one in the morning in an empty house, fine gray fuzz on their shoulders, two feathery moth antennae curling out of their bangs, their pupils glowing red in the reflection, a porch light glowing yellow through the frosted bathroom window, a single vanity bulb, close medium shot into the mirror

choices.label: Pick up the phone and call anyone, just to talk

success.text: You dial the KGLM request line, and a velvet voice answers on the first ring. You talk about nothing: records, cereal, whether moths have favorite songs. Every minute on the line, the antennae shrink a little, and by the time you hang up the fuzz brushes off your shoulders like pollen. The cure for being unwatched, it turns out, is somebody listening.
success.art: A smiling teenager on a kitchen wall phone late at night twirling the curly cord, gray fuzz brushing off their shoulders like pollen, tiny feathery antennae shrinking from their bangs, a radio glowing on the counter

failure.text: Busy signal. Busy signal. Nobody home. You end up on the porch under the light without remembering how you got there, and across the street the Mothman lands on a roof and watches you, head tilted, like a cousin waiting for you to come along.
failure.art: A teenager with feathery antennae standing under a glowing porch light at night, gray dust on their shoulders, a giant moth creature perched on a rooftop across the street tilting its head

choices.label: Put the fuzz under your old science-fair microscope

success.text: Under the lens it is not moth fuzz at all. It is glitter, fountain grime and the dust off dead neon, the stuff of a thousand Saturday afternoons spent waiting at the mall. This is not a mutation. It is loneliness, and loneliness washes off. You scrub until the sink runs gray and the antennae fall out like loose hairs.
success.art: A teenager peering into a small science-fair microscope on a bathroom counter at night, a slide of glittering gray dust under the lens, feathery antennae dropping into the sink

failure.text: The longer you study it, the more it spreads, down your arms and across your knuckles, soft as felt. You sneeze, and a gray cloud fills the bathroom and swirls toward the night-light. You sleep under three blankets and wake with dust on your pillow.
failure.art: A teenager sneezing a billowing cloud of gray moth dust in a small bathroom at night, the cloud swirling toward a glowing night-light, soft gray fuzz spreading down their arms

choices.label: Turn on every light and throw a one-person dance party

success.text: If you are going to be drawn to the light, it will be on your own terms. Every lamp on, the mixtape cranked, you dance through every room in your socks. When your family gets home at two, they find you breathless and laughing on the living room floor, and the antennae are lying on the carpet like two lost feathers.
success.art: A teenager dancing wildly in socks through a brightly lit 1980s living room late at night, every lamp blazing, a boombox on the coffee table, two feathery antennae lying on the shag carpet

failure.text: Every light blazing makes your house a beacon. Something enormous lands on the porch with a thump that rattles the windows, and dust drifts down past the living room curtains. You switch off every lamp and hide under the dining table until dawn, listening to it breathe.
failure.art: A teenager hiding under a dining table in a dark 1980s living room, gray dust drifting past the curtains, the huge shadow of moth wings spread across the front window

signature.title: The Dead Wing
signature.place: Moonbeam Court, Starlight Mall, after midnight
signature.text: You slip behind the plywood into Moonbeam Court. The neon signs are dead, but they hum. From every one of them hang soft gray cocoons, dozens, swaying like paper lanterns, and through the silk you can see sleeping faces: Marcy Holcomb, Tyler Gaskins, kids you have seen at the arcade a hundred times and never once learned the names of. On the dead sign of the Woolmart department store, the Mothman watches you with its clock-face eyespots, wings slowly opening.
signature.art: A boarded-up 1970s mall wing after midnight, rows of dead neon storefront tubes with dozens of soft gray silk cocoons hanging from them and swaying, sleeping children's faces faintly visible through the silk, a drained tiled fountain in the middle, and on top of the big dead department store neon a giant moth with dusty gray-green wings marked with round clock-face eyespots slowly opening, a teenager with a flashlight below, cold moonlight from the skylight, wide shot

choices.label: Climb the dead neon and cut Marcy's cocoon down

success.text: The silk is soft as lint and tougher than rope. You saw through it with a car key and catch Marcy as she slides out. She blinks up at you. "Is it closing time?" Above you the Mothman does not attack. It just watches you hold her, and its wings fold, slowly, like a parent who has been relieved of a shift.
success.art: A teenager on a dead neon sign catching a sleepy little girl sliding out of a gray silk cocoon, a giant moth watching from a nearby sign with its wings folding

failure.text: The sign groans and drops a foot, and you cling to dead neon tubes while the Mothman unfolds above you, all wings and red light. It does not strike. It simply begins, very gently, to spin silk around your ankles. You kick free and run, and you do not stop until the parking lot.
failure.art: A teen dangling from a sagging neon sign with gray silk wrapping around their ankles, a huge moth spreading its wings above in red light

choices.label: Stand at the drained fountain and read the kids' names out loud

success.text: You call every name you know. Marcy. Tyler. Benji. Then every name from Earl's logbook you can remember. With each one, a cocoon stirs, and a sleepy voice says "Here" like attendance. The Mothman tilts its huge head, listening, as if it has been waiting years for someone to say them.
success.art: A teenager standing in a drained wishing fountain full of quarters calling out names, gray cocoons stirring overhead, a giant moth tilting its head to listen

failure.text: You open your mouth and realize you do not know their names. Not one of them. You have seen these kids every Saturday of your life. The Mothman's eyespots glow brighter, and the cocoons sway a little higher, out of reach.
failure.art: A stricken teen standing silent in a drained fountain, cocoons rising higher toward the skylight, a giant moth's eyespots glowing brighter

signature.title: Help Me
signature.text: Your porch light is swarming with little gray moths, more than you have ever seen, and when you step out to shoo them, you hear it: a tiny, thin voice, like a kid talking through a paper-towel tube. "Help me. Help me." It is coming from one moth, bigger than the rest, clinging to the screen door on pale green wings. Up and down Crystal Street, every porch light has the same swarm, and far off over the rooftops something much bigger is circling the town, slowly, as if it is counting.
signature.art: A suburban porch at eleven at night with the porch light swarmed by hundreds of small gray moths, one large pale green luna moth clinging to the screen door, a teenager in a sweatshirt leaning close to it with cupped hands, and far above the rooftops against the full moon a huge winged shadow circling, yellow porch light and blue night, medium shot

choices.label: Cup the moth in your hands and listen closely

success.text: It sits still in your cupped palms, light as a dry leaf, and up close the little voice is clearer: "I wish somebody would come get me. I wish somebody would come." It is a kid's wish, the kind tossed into a fountain with a last quarter. You open your hands, it flutters off toward the dark mall on the hill, and now you know where to look.
success.art: A teenager on a porch at night gently cupping a glowing pale green moth in their palms and listening close, a swarm of gray moths around the porch light, a dark shopping mall on a distant hill

failure.text: The moth bursts into a puff of gray dust in your hands, and the whole swarm lifts off the light and whirls around your head, a hundred tiny voices whispering help me, help me. You slam the door and sit against it until they go quiet.
failure.art: A teenager engulfed in a whirling cloud of gray moths on a porch at night, a puff of dust bursting from their open hands, the screen door swinging, the porch light flickering

choices.label: Catch it in a jar for Bea's monster notebook

success.text: You trap it under a pickle jar, and Bea arrives in her pajamas with a notebook and a magnifying glass. "Wings made of lint," she reports. "Body made of pennies, all from 1974 to 1983, the years Moonbeam Court was open." You let it go, and Bea underlines her notes three times.
success.alone: You trap it under a pickle jar and fetch the monster notebook and a magnifying glass. Wings made of lint. Body made of pennies, all from 1974 to 1983, the years Moonbeam Court was open. You let it go, and underline your notes three times.
success.art: A young girl in pajamas peering through a magnifying glass at a pale green moth inside a pickle jar on a porch at night, a teenager holding a flashlight, an open notebook full of sketches

failure.text: The jar fogs over from the inside, and when it clears, the moth is gone and the jar is full of fine gray dust and one old quarter. Out on the street, every porch light flickers at once.
failure.art: A pickle jar full of swirling gray dust and a single old quarter on a porch railing at night, a startled teenager, every porch light down the suburban street flickering together

choices.label: Switch off the porch light and see where the swarm goes

success.text: You flip the switch, and the swarm lifts off your porch in a gray ribbon and streams down the street from light to light, all flowing one way: toward the dark bulk of Starlight Mall on the hill. From the corner, you watch a shape the size of a car settle onto the mall roof.
success.art: A long ribbon of gray moths streaming down a suburban street at night from porch light to porch light toward a dark shopping mall on a hill, a huge winged shape landing on its roof

failure.text: The swarm does not leave. It pours through the gap under the door and fills your front hall, softly batting at the lamps, until you turn on every light in the house to coax it back outside. Your family comes home to a house lit up like a stadium.
failure.art: A suburban front hall filled with fluttering gray moths batting at lamps, a teenager switching on every light, a house blazing like a stadium on a dark street

signature.title: Paging You
signature.text: The food court is closing, chairs going up on tables, when the PA chimes and says your name. Your full name. "Will someone here for this child please come to the Moonbeam Fountain." The last few shoppers turn to look at you, then look away, and the chime plays again. Gray dust begins to sift down from the skylight onto your tray, and behind the plywood wall of the dead wing, something large shifts its wings, waiting to see who comes.
signature.art: A nearly empty mall food court at 8:55 at night, chairs turned upside down on the tables, a lone teenager sitting at one table with a food tray looking up at a ceiling speaker, gray dust drifting down from a skylight onto the tray, a tall plywood wall at the end of the court with the edges of huge dusty wings shifting behind it, a security guard pushing a mop far away, dimming yellow light, wide shot

choices.label: Grab the information desk mic and page every one of your friends

success.text: You vault the information counter and key the mic: "Will every single one of my friends please report to the food court immediately. This is an emergency of the heart." Within four minutes your crew comes skidding in from the arcade and the parking lot, and the shoppers who watched you get paged start laughing and clapping. Behind the plywood, the shape folds its wings and settles, disappointed.
success.art: A teenager grinning into a microphone at a mall information desk, a crew of friends skidding into the food court from every direction, shoppers clapping, huge wings folding behind a plywood wall

failure.text: The mic squeals with feedback, and the PA swallows your voice and plays the chime instead, over and over, while nobody comes. The dust on your tray thickens into a soft gray blanket, and you have to shake yourself awake on a bench by the drained fountain at midnight.
failure.art: A teenager waking on a bench beside a drained mall fountain at midnight under a soft blanket of gray dust, dead neon tubes overhead, a microphone cord dangling from a dark information desk

choices.label: Walk to the fountain yourself and answer: "I'm here"

success.text: If somebody has to show up for you, it can be you. You walk past the plywood into the dark of Moonbeam Court, stand at the dusty fountain and say, loud and clear, "I'm here." Far above, two red eyes blink in surprise, the PA goes silent, and you walk back to the food court taller than you walked in.
success.art: A teenager standing tall beside a dry dusty fountain in a dark abandoned mall wing, dead neon tubes overhead, two huge red eyes blinking in surprise high in the shadows

failure.text: You stand at the fountain and say it, and your voice sounds very small in the empty court. The PA answers in a buzzing whisper: "Nobody comes. Stay." Gray silk drifts down around your shoulders, and you have to tear free and run.
failure.art: A small teenager beside a dry fountain in a vast dark mall wing, soft gray silk drifting down around their shoulders, red eyes glowing in the rafters, dust in the air

choices.label: Follow the PA wires back to where the page is coming from

success.text: You trace the speaker wire through a ceiling panel and down a service hall to the old Lost Kids desk behind the plywood, where a dusty microphone sits beside a coffee cup still ringed from 1983. On the sign-in sheet, the newest line is written in fresh gray dust, and it is your name. You wipe it away with your sleeve and write underneath: PICKED UP.
success.art: A teenager with a flashlight writing on a dusty clipboard at an abandoned lost children desk in a dark mall wing, an old microphone and a stained coffee cup beside it, dust swirling in the beam

failure.text: The wire leads deep into the service halls and simply ends, cut clean, in a room full of lost-and-found jackets in kid sizes. The page goes on and on over your head, and you find your way out through the loading dock very late and very shaken.
failure.art: A teenager with a flashlight in a dim storage room crowded with racks of small children's jackets, a cut speaker wire dangling from the ceiling, dust drifting in the beam

signature.title: Parents' Night Out
signature.text: Every grown-up on Crystal Street is across town at the Elks Lodge Halloween Ball, and every kid on Crystal Street is home alone with a TV dinner. At eleven the moon goes out. It is not clouds: it is moths, millions of them, a gray storm pouring down out of the sky, and gliding at its center on wings as wide as a garage is the Mothman, eyespots glowing like clocks stuck at closing time. One by one, porch lights flick on as little kids open their front doors to see what is out there.
signature.art: A colossal storm of millions of gray moths pouring down from the sky over a suburban cul-de-sac at eleven at night and covering the moon, a giant moth creature with dusty gray-green wings as wide as a garage and glowing clock-face eyespots gliding at the center, small children in pajamas opening their front doors under porch lights to look up, a teenager running across a lawn waving, dark gray sky and yellow porch lights, wide shot

choices.label: Round up every kid on the street for one giant sleepover

success.text: You run door to door with a bag of glow bracelets, and soon every kid on Crystal Street is in your living room in pajamas, wearing a bracelet, eating popcorn in a blanket fort. Nobody is alone, so nobody is the Mothman's. It lands on your roof, peers in the window at the whole glowing pile of you, and after a long while lifts off and takes the storm with it.
success.art: A living room blanket fort packed with children in pajamas wearing glow bracelets and eating popcorn, a teenager in the middle, a giant moth with glowing eyespots peering curiously through the window

failure.text: You get most of them, but when you count heads in your living room you come up one short. Through the window you see a small figure in footie pajamas crossing the roundabout, looking up, and you catch them just as the storm of wings brushes past you both.
failure.art: A teenager sprinting across a suburban roundabout at night to scoop up a small child in footie pajamas, a storm of gray moth wings brushing past them, a glowing purple geode nearby

choices.label: Borrow Wade's van and drag every parent home from the Elks Lodge

success.text: Wade floors it across town, and you burst into the Halloween Ball in the middle of the costume conga, shouting that the kids are alone and the sky is full of moths. Parents in vampire capes and witch hats look at each other, then pile into the van, their station wagons and anything with wheels. The convoy roars down Crystal Street with every headlight blazing, and the swarm scatters like gray mist.
success.alone: The keys are under the van's visor where they always are, and you lurch it across town in second gear and burst into the Halloween Ball in the middle of the costume conga, shouting that the kids are alone and the sky is full of moths. Parents in vampire capes and witch hats look at each other, then pile into the van, their station wagons and anything with wheels. The convoy roars down Crystal Street with every headlight blazing, and the swarm scatters like gray mist.
success.art: A convoy of station wagons and a battered van roaring down a suburban street at night with headlights blazing, parents in vampire capes and witch hats leaning out the windows, a swarm of moths scattering

failure.text: The DJ is too loud, the parents are too busy dancing, and nobody hears a word you shout. You drive back alone to find the street smothered in drifting gray dust and every porch light blinking.
failure.art: A teenager shouting unheard in a crowded lodge hall full of dancing adults in Halloween costumes, a mirror ball spinning, a disco DJ booth, gray dust drifting past the windows

choices.label: Build a decoy light on the roundabout to pull the swarm away from the houses

success.text: You drag every lamp and flashlight you can find onto the roundabout, wire them to a car battery and throw the switch. The Heartstone blazes like a lighthouse in a ring of bulbs, and the swarm swings away from the porches and spirals around it, while the Mothman circles above them all until dawn, dazzled and harmless.
success.art: A ring of mismatched lamps and flashlights wired to a car battery blazing around a purple geode on a roundabout at night, a spiral of gray moths and a giant moth creature circling above, dazzled

failure.text: The car battery sparks, every bulb pops at once, and the street goes dark except for the porches where little kids still stand in their doorways, lit up. You spend the night running from house to house, shooing children back inside.
failure.art: Popped light bulbs smoking around a dark roundabout at night, a sparking car battery, little children silhouetted in lit doorways down the street, a teenager running between houses

finale.title: Last Call at Moonbeam Court
finale.place: Moonbeam Court, Starlight Mall, Halloween night
finale.text: On Halloween night every dead sign in Moonbeam Court blazes back to life, pink and green and gold, and the drained fountain fills with dust instead of water. The Mothman spreads its wings across the whole court, eyespots ticking like clocks that never reach morning. Dozens of cocoons sway beneath it. "They wait," it hums through the old PA speakers, "and nobody comes. So I come. Who is coming for you?"
finale.art: A boarded-up 1970s mall court on Halloween night blazing with revived pink, green and gold neon storefronts, a giant moth with dusty gray-green wings spread across the entire court, round clock-face eyespots on the wings and two glowing red eyes, dozens of gray silk cocoons hanging beneath it, a drained fountain filled with glittering gray dust, four teenagers in homemade Halloween costumes facing it with flashlights raised, neon glow, low wide shot

choices.label: Bring down the Woolmart sign with the creature on it

success.text: You climb the scaffolding and smash the bolts until the giant sign groans, tilts and falls in a shower of sparks. The Mothman bursts into a cloud of dust and moth wings, and the cocoons tear open one by one, spilling sleepy kids onto the tiles. Nobody is hurt. Nobody is quite sure what happened, either.
success.art: A giant neon department store sign crashing down in sparks, a moth creature exploding into a cloud of dust and wings, cocoons tearing open and dropping sleepy kids onto mall tiles

failure.text: The sign holds. The Mothman's wings fold around you like a blanket, soft and warm and smelling of popcorn and chlorine, and a voice inside your head says it's all right, it's all right, nobody will notice you're gone.
failure.art: A teen being enfolded in giant dusty moth wings like a blanket under glowing neon, silk beginning to wrap around them

choices.label: Rewire the mall's rooftop sign into the brightest light in Glimmer Falls

success.text: You splice every circuit in the dead wing into the giant STARLIGHT sign on the roof and throw the switch. The night goes white. The Mothman cannot help it: it rises through the skylight toward the blaze and circles it, dazzled, while your crew cuts down every cocoon below. By dawn it is a speck spiraling toward the moon.
success.art: A giant rooftop mall sign blazing white against the night sky, a huge moth circling it in a dazzled spiral, teens below cutting down cocoons inside through the skylight

failure.text: The circuit blows. Every light in Starlight Mall goes out, and in the perfect dark, the only lights left are two red eyes, coming closer, and the soft sound of silk being spun.
failure.art: A pitch-dark mall with only two glowing red eyes visible approaching a teen holding a smoking fuse box, faint silk strands catching starlight

choices.label: Get on the old PA and page every parent in Glimmer Falls by name

success.text: KGLM patches into the mall PA, and you read from Earl's logbook, Kev's envelope and Mona's wishes. "Will the parents of Marcy Holcomb please come to the Moonbeam Fountain. Will the parents of Tyler Gaskins. Will the parents of Benji Ferreira." One by one, in pajamas, in uniforms, in curlers, they come running through the plywood. Every time a grown-up says "I'm here," a cocoon opens. The Mothman folds its wings and watches them hold on.
success.art: Parents in pajamas and work uniforms running into a neon-lit abandoned mall wing, cocoons opening to release sleepy children into their arms, a teen at an old PA microphone reading from a logbook, a giant moth folding its wings above

failure.text: The PA crackles and squeals. Your words come out as static, and the old speakers only play the chime, over and over, the closing-time chime. Nobody comes. The Mothman hums sadly. It knew they would not.
failure.art: A teen gripping a crackling PA microphone, old ceiling speakers spitting static, an empty plywood gap, a doorway left vacant, a giant moth bowing its head

choices.label: Make it see that somebody is watching now, the way you learned on the first nights

success.text: On the first nights you learned what it wants: a kid nobody is watching. So you hand every friend a flashlight, post one under each cocoon with the beam pointed up, and call out the kids' names over a walkie. With every cocoon watched and nothing left to keep, the Mothman lets the silk go one cocoon at a time and drifts up through the skylight toward the moon.
success.art: Teens standing under swaying gray cocoons in a neon-lit mall court shining flashlight beams upward, cocoons opening to release sleepy kids, a giant moth creature drifting up through a skylight toward the moon

failure.text: There are more cocoons than flashlights, and the Mothman's eyespots follow the ones left in the dark. Some of the silk loosens, but not enough. You know how this works; find more people to watch.
failure.art: A few flashlight beams pointing at a forest of swaying gray cocoons in a dim mall court, many cocoons left in shadow, a giant moth creature's glowing eyespots watching the dark ones

choices.label: Stand under its wings and refuse it, the way you stood your ground when it came for your street

success.text: It came for your street and your town, and you stood your ground every time. You climb onto the fountain rim, plant your feet under its enormous wings and shout, "Not one more kid. I'm here, and they're with me," as your crew climbs up beside you. The Mothman rears, then folds, pushed back by a wall of people who showed up, and the cocoons split, spilling sleepy kids onto the tiles.
success.art: A teenager and their crew standing defiantly on the rim of a dusty mall fountain beneath the vast spread wings of a giant moth creature, the creature rearing back, gray cocoons splitting open behind it

failure.text: You climb onto the rim, but a downdraft of dusty wings knocks you flat into the drained fountain. You were right to stand there. Get back up; your crew is coming.
failure.art: A teenager knocked flat into a drained dusty fountain by a gust from enormous moth wings, neon glowing pink and green overhead, friends running toward the fountain

choices.label: Page every parent by name, the way you refused to let anyone be alone the night before

success.text: The night before Halloween you proved that nobody on this street had to be alone, and now you prove it to the whole town. You read the names from Earl's logbook, Kev's envelope and Mona's wishes over the old PA, and parents come running through the plywood in pajamas, uniforms and curlers. Every time a grown-up says "I'm here," a cocoon opens, and the Mothman folds its wings and watches them hold on.
success.art: Parents in pajamas, work uniforms and curlers running into a neon-lit mall court to hug sleepy children spilling from opened gray cocoons, a teenager at an old microphone, a giant moth folding its wings above

failure.text: You read the names, but the old PA crackles and drops half of them into static, and only a few grown-ups make it through the plywood. Keep reading. The rest are on their way.
failure.art: A teenager reading names into a crackling old microphone in a dim mall court, a handful of parents squeezing through a gap in a plywood wall, many gray cocoons still hanging overhead

best.title: Someone Is Coming
best.text: The last cocoon opens when Earl Lusk walks in, blazer on, and lifts a kid nobody else came for onto his shoulders. With no child left unwatched in Moonbeam Court, the Mothman settles onto the empty fountain, folds its wings, and settles into a soft gray drift in the shape of Mona's wings. By spring the town has hauled the real Mona back from Rusty's Junkyard, twenty feet of fiberglass, smiling, and set her over a refilled fountain in a reopened Moonbeam Court, where the old Lost Kids desk now has a new sign, MOONBEAM CLUB, FREE TILL CLOSING, and Earl behind it with a sign-in sheet and a coffee. Parents on Crystal Street start a babysitting swap. Kev starts knocking on doors when the papers pile up. And kids still throw quarters in Mona's fountain, but now they mostly wish for pizza.
best.art: A reopened 1970s mall court in daylight, a restored twenty-foot fiberglass luna moth with pale green wings and a painted smile standing over a sparkling refilled fountain, a 70-year-old Black man in a navy security blazer at a desk signing in laughing kids, parents and children everywhere, coins glinting in the fountain water, bright skylight sun, wide shot

good.title: Pest Control
good.text: The cocoons are cut down and the kids go home, groggy and fine. The Mothman is gone, or at least nobody sees it again. The mall puts up a new plywood wall and calls it a gas leak. The next Saturday, the arcade is full of the same kids, parked there at ten, waiting for closing, and you notice them now. You are not sure anyone else does.
good.art: A crowded mall arcade on a Saturday morning, kids alone at the glowing machines with their coats still on, a new plywood wall in the background with a faint dusty outline of moth wings on it, a teenager leaning against a cabinet watching the kids thoughtfully, arcade light, medium wide shot

bittersweet.title: One Cocoon Left
bittersweet.text: You free almost all of them. But when the lights come up on November first, one gray cocoon still hangs from the dead Woolmart sign, too high to reach, and the Mothman is curled around it. The mall boards the wing up again that winter, tighter than before. Every Saturday you check the logbook names against the kids at the arcade, and every Saturday you hope you are wrong about who is missing.
bittersweet.art: A single gray silk cocoon hanging high from a dead neon department store tube in a dark mall wing, a giant moth with dusty gray-green wings curled around it, and at the entrance two workers nailing fresh plywood boards over the opening, a teenager watching through the last gap, thin gray winter light, wide shot

bad.title: Nobody Noticed
bad.text: You wake in the dark, wrapped in soft gray silk, warm and drowsy, hanging from a dead neon sign. It is not bad in here. It is quiet. The Mothman watches over you. It takes your family three days to notice you are gone, and that, more than the cocoon, is the part your crew never forgives this town for. They are still trying to cut you down.
bad.art: A teenager asleep inside a translucent gray silk cocoon hanging from a dead neon tube in an abandoned mall wing, a giant moth with dusty wings and glowing red eyes perched beside it keeping watch, three friends with flashlights and box cutters climbing a metal scaffold toward the cocoon, flashlight beams in the dark, wide shot
